notes.subject: language
notes.text: A unique non-Latin alphabet with softer lowercase shapes than Cyrillic; also used on the island nation to the east.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Plates are all white or standard EU style with a blue strip on the left; taxis have yellow plates.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Mostly wooden poles, often dark brown and noticeably taller than elsewhere.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Harp-shaped metal frame pole tops, unique to this country and one island neighbour; many poles carry five vertical insulators.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: A small lamp with a round shade above the bulb hangs from the side of poles.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Slightly faded solid white double middle lines are common, setting it apart from most Mediterranean countries.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Yellow road lines are more common than in any other southern European country.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Wedge-shaped bollards with almost square reflectors, red on the front and white on the back.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons have white arrows on black; the western neighbour uses the same but with only two or four arrows.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Warning signs have a red border and a yellow background.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Blue arrow-shaped direction signs with place names in a yellow font in the local script and white in English.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Town entry signs are white with thick horizontal blue stripes at the top and bottom.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Blue kilometre markers with km written on the left in both scripts.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Pedestrian signs show two dotted horizontal lines instead of stripes.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Miniature churches on small pedestals along roads are unique to this country.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: White and pastel stone houses with orange tiled roofs, multi-floor light apartment blocks with connected balconies; white houses are more common than in other Mediterranean countries.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: White houses with blue fences, frames and doors are the iconic style, mainly on islands.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Very mountainous, with much coverage on winding mountain roads and plenty of red dirt.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Includes smallcam coverage, and plenty of bleak winter and autumn generation 3; unlike the island neighbour, no antenna is visible on smallcam.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Many small islands have patchy coverage; only the mainland and the biggest southern island have all three camera generations.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Area codes start with 2 followed by 1 to 3 digits; a third digit of 1 means the regional main city and 9 its surroundings.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The largest flat farm valleys are near Thessaloniki and Larissa; smaller ones with closer mountains occur across the north and centre.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The tallest mountains and most high-altitude roads are in the western half.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Completely white houses with blue doors and shutters are mainly on the small central Cyclades.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Many central islands are barren, with small bushes and no trees, especially smaller ones with coverage.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Olive groves are along the coast, notably in the big southern island and southern Peloponnese; citrus groves mainly in southern Peloponnese.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: A car antenna with a slight bulge at the tip is unique to the large southern island.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Mount Pangaion is a solitary mountain just south of a flat farm valley.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Giant monolithic rock pillars called Meteora rise north of Trikala.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Yellow taxis are in the capital; blue taxis with white roofs in Thessaloniki, where many unusually tall rooftop antennas also appear.
